message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas

- **Van Gogh**: fits a restorer's eye for craft
- **The Dovetail Express**
- **Sir Loads-a-Lot**
- **Chester** (as in chest of drawers)

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

This is the **only order that works**. B has to be first to finish before it opens at 09:30. Going to A first gets the driver to B at 09:40 at the earliest. C has to be last because it won't accept anything before 11:00.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B, unload 08:50–09:05 (done well before 09:30 opening) |
| 09:05 | Drive to A (25 min) |
| 09:30 | Arrive A, unload 09:30–09:45 (inside 09:00–10:00 window) |
| 09:45 | Drive to C (40 min) |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C. **30-minute break, 10:25–10:55** |
| 11:00 | Unload at C, 11:00–11:15 |
| 11:15 | Drive back to depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot, exactly on the deadline** |

The break fits naturally, because the driver arrives at C 35 minutes before it will accept the delivery.

**The return has no slack at all.** Unloading at C can't start before 11:00, and the drive back takes 45 minutes. Any delay at C, such as a slow handover or an unload running past 15 minutes, makes him late back. To protect it:
- **Ask C whether they'll accept at 10:45.** Even 15 minutes earlier gives you real margin.
- If they won't, make sure C knows to be ready **at 11:00 sharp**, and have the driver load C's items so they come off easily.
- Check that the 45-minute return from C is realistic around midday traffic. I've assumed it matches the outbound time.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> "Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Business]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!"

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition:** no new scratches, dents or marks on the finish. Check together with the customer.
2. **Function:** doors, drawers and hinges open smoothly, and the piece stands level and steady.
3. **Completeness:** it's the right item, with all parts, keys, shelves and fittings included.

## Delivery note: email, with a paper copy on request

- **Default to email.** Capture the signature on a phone or tablet, then email the note. That gives you a record that can't get lost.
- **Offer paper** to customers who prefer it.

## Proof of delivery, in one line

> **Proof of delivery:** a signed and dated record that the customer received the item in good condition. It's our evidence if there's any dispute later.

## Evening-before text, under 160 characters

> "Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] arrives tomorrow, approx [9:30-10:30]. We'll text when the driver sets off. Reply with any questions. Thanks!"

The fixed text is **123 characters**, leaving **37 characters** for the name, business name and time combined. For example, "Sarah", "Oak & Ash Restoration" and "9:30-10:30" come to 36.

**Avoid emoji and curly apostrophes.** A single emoji, or a "smart" apostrophe in "We'll", makes the phone switch character encoding and cuts the single-message limit from 160 characters to **70**. Type a plain straight apostrophe, or check that your texting system doesn't convert it automatically.
